nameStory: The Many-colored Tellin gets its name from the beautiful array of colors that can appear on its shell - from pale pink and yellow to lavender and white, often with subtle bands or rays. The word 'tellin' comes from the Greek word for 'far off,' possibly referring to how these clams can extend their long feeding tubes far from their buried shells. Each individual shell seems to have its own unique color palette, making every find a little surprise!
description: The Many-colored Tellin is a small, flattened clam that lives buried in sandy beaches along the coast. Its smooth, oval shell typically measures about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, with a distinctly compressed, thin profile. The shell's surface gleams with a polished appearance and displays various pastel colors - you might find shells that are peachy-pink, pale yellow, lavender, or creamy white. Like other tellins, this clam has two matching shell halves (called valves) that are hinged together.

idTips.label: Shell shape and size
idTips.description: Look for a small, distinctly flattened oval shell about the size of your thumbnail, feeling thin and delicate when you pick it up

idTips.label: Variable coloration
idTips.description: Notice the range of soft pastel colors - shells may be pink, yellow, lavender, or white, sometimes with faint radiating lines or bands

idTips.label: Surface texture
idTips.description: Run your finger across the smooth, polished surface that feels almost glossy, with very fine growth lines you can barely feel

idTips.label: Shell profile
idTips.description: View the shell from the side to see how compressed and thin it appears, much flatter than most other small clams

idTips.label: Hinge area
idTips.description: Examine the pointed end where you'll find small teeth and the ligament that held the two shell halves together

habitat: Many-colored Tellins live in sandy or muddy-sand areas of protected bays, estuaries, and calmer coastal waters throughout New England. You'll most likely find their empty shells washed up on sandy beaches, especially after storms, though the living clams remain buried several inches deep in the sediment. They prefer areas where the salinity is fairly consistent, often in the same habitats where you might find soft-shell clams and razor clams.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after spring storms, often mixed with other small shells and seaweed. This is when winter storm damage brings up shells from deeper waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for beach exploration when empty shells are most visible on clean, dry sand during low tide walks.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity increases shell deposits on beaches, and the living clams are actively feeding in the sediment before winter.
seasonality.winter: Shells become buried under storm debris and sand, though the living clams remain active in deeper, more stable sediment layers.

funFact: Many-colored Tellins can actually change the color intensity of their shells based on their diet and environment - a clam living in iron-rich sediments might develop more vibrant pink or orange tones, while one in different conditions stays pale yellow or white!
confusionNotes: The Many-colored Tellin is most easily confused with other small tellin clams, but its distinctly flattened profile and variable pastel colors set it apart from rounder clam shells. Remember: 'Thin tellins' - the flattened shape is your best clue that you've found a tellin rather than a quahog, soft-shell clam, or other rounder bivalve.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertain claim flagged**: With only one recorded observation in New England, this species may be at the northern edge of its range or possibly misidentified in regional records. The identification and distribution information should be considered preliminary until more specimens can confirm the species' presence in New England waters.
compareHints: The Many-colored Tellin differs from its close relative the Northern Dwarf-tellin by typically being slightly larger and showing more diverse coloration patterns. **Uncertain claim flagged**: The Northern Dwarf-tellin tends to be smaller and more consistently pale or white, lacking the pink and lavender tones often seen in Many-colored Tellins. Both share the characteristic flattened tellin shape, but the color variation is usually the best distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Northern Dwarf-tellin is generally smaller and paler than its relative the Many-colored Tellin, which tends to have more pink, orange, or purple tinting.
